t: Paragraph (2) of section 3704(c) is amended to read as follows:“(2) In any case in which a veteran is in active-duty status as a member of the Armed Forces and is unable to occupy a property because of such status, the occupancy requirements of this chapter shall be considered to be satisfied if—“(A) the spouse of the veteran occupies or intends to occupy the property as a home and the spouse makes the certification required by paragraph (1) of this subsection; or“(B) a dependent child of the veteran occupies or will occupy the property as a home and the veteran’s attorney-in-fact or legal guardian of the dependent child makes the certification required by paragraph (1) of this subsection.”.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that a spouse or attorney-in-fact making a certification to the government is outside-party involvement. But this is only an occupancy certification made as part of obtaining a VA home loan benefit, which is an application-type requirement and not consultation or input into a federal decision. The section provides for no comment period, hearing, advisory body, rulemaking, or right to sue.
fable.s: the spouse of the veteran occupies or intends to occupy the property as a home and the spouse makes the certification required by paragraph (1) of this subsection

opus.w: This section only explains how a veteran on active duty can meet the occupancy requirement for a VA home loan: a spouse, or the attorney-in-fact or guardian of a dependent child, makes a certification. It might look like participation because people outside the government give information to the VA. But that certification is part of applying for a benefit, which the definition excludes. No outsider is consulted on a federal policy decision, and the section has no comment period, hearing, advisory body, or right to sue.
opus.s: the spouse of the veteran occupies or intends to occupy the property as a home and the spouse makes the certification required by paragraph (1) of this subsection

qwen_chat.w: This section outlines conditions under which occupancy requirements for a benefit are considered satisfied. The certifications provided by spouses, children, or guardians are part of the eligibility determination for a benefit. The definition explicitly excludes 'applications for benefits or grants' from the scope of participation. Therefore, this is not participation.
qwen_chat.s: the occupancy requirements of this chapter shall be considered to be satisfied if—“(A) the spouse of the veteran occupies or intends to occupy the property as a home and the spouse makes the certification required by paragraph (1) of this subsection; or“(B) a dependent child of the veteran occupies or will occupy the property as a home and the veteran’s attorney-in-fact or legal guardian of the dependent child makes the certification required by paragraph (1) of this subsection.”
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that the involvement of a spouse, dependent child, or attorney-in-fact constitutes "participation" because these are non-federal actors making certifications. However, this is incorrect because the section describes the criteria for satisfying occupancy requirements for a benefit (likely a tax exemption or loan program). The definition explicitly states: "It does not include applications for benefits or grants." The certification is part of the application/eligibility process for a benefit, not a consultation or coordination process where the government seeks input from outsiders before making a policy or administrative decision. The actors are providing information to prove eligibility, not participating in the decision-making process itself.
